def rz(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=np.float64); med = np.median(x)
    mad = np.median(np.abs(x - med)) * 1.4826 + 1e-12
    return (x - med) / mad

The plateau is not a content-dependent circuit. Zeroing it changes the residual after layer 9 by about 12–14% of its norm (mean change ≈ 780), and that change points in nearly the same direction at every token. The norm of the mean write is 0.83–0.91 of the mean per-token norm, in gold math, own answers and chats alike, in prompts and answers. So the rank-16 component writes a near-constant, bias-like vector at all positions, most plausibly by mapping the attention-sink (BOS) value that every position attends to.

That explains the earlier results. It is not math-gated, so it is inert on gold math and on chats under the flatten, and full removal (E19) hurts broadly: operand −0.08, result −0.10, non-math −0.055, own answers −0.11. Because attention output is RMS-normalised after o_proj, a large constant component also scales down layer 9's natural attention signal. Removing it boosts layer 9's copy heads, which fits the extra looping.

To pin down what this constant is, I'll check which residual channels the mean write occupies:
- an outlier/massive channel would mean normalisation machinery;
- a diffuse direction would make it a steering vector.

I'll also check whether the direction is the same across groups. Logit-lens it as well: if it were a planted bias, it should push specific token classes, such as termination tokens or digits.

The last result shows that the plateau's mean write is almost entirely (94%) on residual channel 163, one of the massive outlier channels. The direction is the same for gold math, the model's own answers and chats (cos 0.96–0.995). The logit-lens numbers are not meaningful for a massive-channel vector, because the final norm dominates them.

So the rank-16 component in layer 9 o_proj acts mainly on the normalisation/attention-sink lever, not as a math-gated signal. That fits both earlier results: flattening it was neutral pooled over 512 DEV problems, and zeroing it caused broad harm and looping. One open point is whether that channel-163 write is direct, with the plateau's output directions spanning channel 163, or indirect, through post-attention RMSNorm rescaling and the layer-9 MLP. If it is indirect, the plateau's own direct write is the small remaining diffuse part.

I'll check this from the weights alone: the share of channel 163 in each plateau output direction against the bulk, and the post-attention norm gain on that channel. In the same run I'll re-read the start of my notebook, which the restart did not show, to recall every closed line before planning the remaining 21 passes. If channel 163 dominates the plateau's output directions, the plateau is massive-channel machinery and the L9 line is fully closed. If it doesn't, the direct diffuse write is still unexamined.

The key result is that the plateau's output directions contain almost no channel 163 (0.7% of their energy), while layer 9's post-attention norm gain on channel 163 is 450 against a median of about 20. So the "94% on channel 163" write is indirect. The plateau adds a near-constant diffuse vector that inflates the RMS of layer 9's attention output, and the RMSNorm then shrinks the bulk's own channel-163 contribution, which the gain of 450 multiplies.

The plateau therefore acts as an RMS damper on layer 9's attention, the same for every kind of text. That matches what we saw: removing it does not reliably help math (pooled DEV about +0.2 points) and causes looping. I consider the L9 line closed.

The re-read notes also remind me that head ablations in this architecture are confounded by this same post-attention RMS rescaling. The spectral scan only catches low-rank plants. A planted change could also be per-unit: a neuron or head scaled down or up, or zeroed. That leaves no low-rank trace, but it would show up as an outlier in per-unit weight norms, or as exact zeros.

So I'll do a weight-only scan of every layer:
- MLP neurons: robust z-scores of the gate-row, up-row and down-column norms;
- attention: per-head norms of the q/o blocks and the k/v norms;
- exact-zero counts in every matrix.

A planted unit should stand out as an extreme outlier (|z| > 8, or exact zeros) in one or a few layers; a smooth picture closes the per-unit line.

The scan finds no exact zeros, and no attention head is an outlier. Every k/v projection has Frobenius norm ≈ 16, which suggests near-unit rows: uniform and apparently a property of training. The MLPs show something to follow up in the late layers (12–17), in two parts:
- **Heavy gate tail:** many neurons have very large gate-row norms (z up to 45).
- **Up/down low outliers:** some neurons combine a normal or huge gate with tiny up and down weights (z ≈ −7 to −10). Examples are L13 n204 (gate z = +27, up −7.4, down −9.3), L14 n575 and L16 n378.

A neuron that still gates strongly but whose output path (up × down) was shrunk is exactly what a hand-planted attenuation of capability neurons would look like. Natural dead neurons usually shrink in all three matrices together.

To tell these apart, I'll list, per layer, every neuron with a low up or down norm (z < −5) together with its gate z, and the shape of the gate-norm distribution:
- **Planted:** a cluster of such neurons concentrated in some layers, whose gate rows stay normal or large.
- **Natural:** a few scattered neurons that are small in all three matrices, or a smooth heavy tail.
